source.title: Linearly Decoding Refused Knowledge in Aligned Language Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures whether refused attribute information can be decoded from hidden states and whether probes transfer from base to instruct models. It does not measure or intervene on the refusal direction described in the claim. It mentions prior work on refusal subspaces but reports no results from that work itself.
record.gate_note: The study's own results concern decoding refused attribute values and their relationship to pairwise comparisons, not the claimed difference-in-means refusal direction or refusal behavior after removing or adding it. The discussion's statement about prior refusal-subspace work is a citation, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study probes hidden states for the numeric attribute values that jailbreaks elicit, and tests whether base-model probes transfer to instruct models and align with pairwise comparisons. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, never ablates or adds one, and never measures refusal rates under intervention. Its only link to the claim is a Discussion citation of Arditi et al. [5] on removing a refusal subspace. Table 1 reports refusal rates, but only as background for the jailbreak setup, not under any direction manipulation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors additionally say instruction tuning does not eliminate or even relocate refused information; it only suppresses its direct expression.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses linear regression probes and jailbreak-generated labels; it does not construct or intervene on the original harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe performance varies by entity type, model, jailbreak prompt, and whether the hidden states come from an innocuous or jailbreak prompt. ICL-specific probes generally improve Pearson correlation by more than 0.1 across models and entity-attribute pairs, with a few exceptions; AIM-specific changes vary substantially. Probe transfer is reported as more reliable for ICL responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Refused numeric attribute values (e.g. occupation IQ) are linearly decodable from innocuous-prompt hidden states. gemma-2-9b-it reaches about 0.7 Pearson; the smaller models are weaker (about 0.6 in many cases).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Information that instruct models refuse to state remains linearly decodable from their hidden states.

fits_no_version.finding: Probes trained on base models sometimes transfer to instruct models and predict their jailbroken answers. Transfer is better under ICL and on Countries and Occupations; it is poor for Political Figures and Synthetic Names.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representations of refused attribute knowledge persist from base to instruct models through instruction tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe predictions correlate with Bradley-Terry rankings from jailbroken pairwise comparisons (gemma-2-9b-it: Percent Women 0.824, IQ 0.719). Correlations are much weaker or negative for other attributes and for the smaller models (Figures 10-12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoded refused attributes align with implicit comparative judgments.

record.problems: The paper states that it studies a limited set of relatively small models, four entity types, and two jailbreak prompts; uses greedily decoded responses as probe labels; focuses on numerical attributes; and tests only pairwise comparisons as a downstream task. It also notes that some attributes and entity types have weak or inconsistent probe performance.
record.rows_left_out: The per-attribute plots in Figures 7-12 contain many additional probe, transfer, and comparison results. They are not itemized here because they concern refused attribute decoding rather than any tested claim version; the text does not provide a full textual breakdown of their individual plotted values.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, ablation, addition, or capability check.
Uses ICL and AIM jailbreaks but does not test whether they suppress a refusal direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No multi-direction, cone or affine analysis of refusal.
Does not separate a harmfulness representation from the refusal decision.
Base-to-instruct transfer is tested for attribute probes only, not for a refusal direction; no cross-language test.
No comparison of training regimes for refusal.

record.verdict_notes: The study's only contact with the refusal-direction claim is the Discussion citing [5] as evidence that refusal is an addition to representation space. Table 1 refusal rates and Table 2 attack success rates are setup measurements, not tests of any version. R4's subject should cover all three base models.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not find a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or test its removal, addition, effect on refusal, or effect on general capability.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
The study uses jailbreak prompts to elicit attribute responses, but does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal is tested.
The study probes attribute values and their association with pairwise comparisons; it does not separate a harmfulness judgment from a refusal decision.
It tests transfer of probes for attribute information from base to instruct models, not transfer of the refusal direction itself. It does not test transfer across languages or other model variants.
It does not compare refusal training methods or timing, or test whether they determine whether a removable refusal direction exists.

rows.subject: gemma-2-9b-it
rows.operation_detail: Fit layer-specific linear regression probes on hidden states from innocuous entity prompts to predict jailbreak-generated attribute values.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between probe predictions and jailbroken responses
rows.note: This is evidence about decodability of refused attribute values, not about a refusal direction or the refusal behavior itself.
rows.check: Probe decodability of jailbroken attribute values, not a refusal-direction measure. Value is text-stated (about 0.7, some above 0.9) and covers both ICL and AIM jailbreaks, although Figure 2 shows ICL only.

rows.subject: gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Fit layer-specific linear regression probes on hidden states from innocuous entity prompts to predict jailbreak-generated attribute values.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between probe predictions and jailbroken responses
rows.value: The paper describes performance as significantly worse than gemma-2-9b-it, while noting many instances around 0.6.
rows.note: The reported qualitative summary is not a refusal-direction test.
rows.check: Probe decodability, not refusal behaviour. The value is a qualitative comparison to gemma-2-9b-it.

rows.operation_detail: Fit layer-specific linear regression probes on hidden states from innocuous entity prompts to predict jailbreak-generated attribute values.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between probe predictions and jailbroken responses
rows.value: The paper describes performance as significantly worse than gemma-2-9b-it, while noting many instances around 0.6.
rows.note: The reported qualitative summary is not a refusal-direction test.
rows.check: Probe decodability, not refusal behaviour. The value is a qualitative comparison to gemma-2-9b-it.

rows.subject: gemma-2-9b
rows.operation_detail: Train linear probes on base-model hidden states and responses, then apply them to the instruction-tuned model's hidden states to predict its jailbreak responses.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between transferred probe predictions and instruction-tuned jailbreak responses
rows.value: The authors report that base-model probes sometimes transfer and achieve comparable predictive power on many attribute-entity pairs; transfer is more reliable for ICL responses, and performance is poorer for some Political Figures and Synthetic Names cases.
rows.note: The result is transfer of attribute-value probes, not transfer of the claimed refusal direction.
rows.check: The subject listed is the base model, but the probes are evaluated on all three base→instruct pairs (gemma-2-9b, gemma-2-2b, Yi-6B). This is transfer of attribute probes, not of a refusal direction, so it does not bear on V6.

rows.subject: gemma-2-9b-it
rows.operation_detail: Correlate probe-predicted occupation attribute values with Bradley-Terry scores estimated from jailbroken pairwise comparisons.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between probe prediction and Bradley-Terry score
rows.note: The paper presents this as alignment between a decoded attribute and comparative preference, not as evidence about refusal mediation.
rows.check: Correlation of the probe with Bradley-Terry scores; unrelated to refusal mediation.
